Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump announced he had reached a diesel export agreement with Russia and delayed additional sanctions in order to avoid jeopardizing peace negotiations with Ukraine. title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6897 – Reuters estimate
body: The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.--- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary: The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets.

That makes the 28 October inflation data the pivotal event: a hot print would revive November hike pricing quickly, while a soft one would likely cement a pause. title: Only a third of the US data centre pipeline looks credible as AI financing strains build
body: The repricing so far is selective rather than AI-wide: the heaviest pressure falls on companies that need outside capital to build, including Oracle, SoftBank and former bitcoin miners turned AI hosts such as Cipher and TeraWulf, while cash-rich hyperscalers like Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon are far less exposed and some of their shareholders may welcome slower capex. The second-order risk sits with Nvidia and the wider chip supply chain, where part of future demand depends on customers that have yet to secure financing. In Asia, any push-out of orders would show up first in SK Hynix, Samsung and TSMC, a meaningful risk for a chip-heavy Kospi after its strong run. At the index level, the AI build-out has been a key support for US earnings and growth, so even a slowdown rather than a collapse trims a major pillar for broader equities and, through risk sentiment, the Australian dollar. Signs that stress is spreading beyond the neoclouds, such as hyperscaler capex cuts or wider credit spreads, would mark the shift from a sector repricing to a broader market problem. --- Info via FT, (gated) --- Earlier: CoreWeave bonds trade like distressed debt as AI spending outpaces balance sheets --- The AI boom's binding constraint is shifting from chips to permits, power and credit, and investors are beginning to price the gap between announced data centre capacity and what can realistically be financed and built.

title: Australian Dollar Rises from Multi-Month Lows
body: The Australian dollar climbed toward $0.70, rebounding from multi‑month lows as markets digested fresh commentary from the central bank. Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Christopher Kent acknowledged signs that the labor market is cooling faster than anticipated, but warned against placing too much weight on a single month's data. Unemployment unexpectedly rose to 4.7% in September, the highest level in five years, leading markets to pare back expectations for another interest rate increase. Kent also pointed to evidence that neutral interest rates are moving higher both in Australia and globally. He maintained that monetary policy is still somewhat restrictive, while raising the question of whether it is restrictive enough. At the same time, after posting a modest weekly loss, the Australian dollar recovered some ground against the US dollar. The move followed comments from Federal Reserve officials suggesting no immediate pressure to tighten policy. title: Inflation Near 2% as AI Demand Adds Pressure: BoJ Gov Ueda
body: Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament on Monday that underlying inflation is now "quite close" to the central bank's 2% target, with strong global demand for AI-related goods and services adding to price pressures already stemming from a tight labor market. Ueda stressed that it is becoming increasingly important to firmly anchor inflation around 2%. He noted that rising raw material costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East are contributing to higher prices, while demand-driven factors—such as robust employment conditions and an ongoing economic recovery—are also pushing inflation up. Ueda added that raising interest rates at an appropriate pace would help prevent sharp jumps in government bond yields and warned that failing to adjust monetary policy could fuel concerns about an inflation overshoot. Responding to questions on fiscal policy, Ueda said that higher government spending would likely stimulate wages and prices in the short term, though measures that expand the economy's supply capacity could help moderate inflation over the longer run. His comments come ahead of the Bank of Japan's policy meeting later this month, where new projections for growth and inflation will be scrutinized for clues on the timing and pace of future interest rate increases. title: RBA Kent Questions Rate Restraint Despite Four Hikes
body: Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Christopher Kent said in a speech that mounting evidence of rising global neutral interest rates is casting doubt on how restrictive current policy really is, despite four rate hikes this year. While he remains confident that monetary policy is somewhat tight, he questioned whether it is tight enough. A higher neutral rate implies that the current 4.6% cash rate may be putting less downward pressure on demand and inflation than policymakers had assumed. This, in turn, strengthens the case for keeping interest rates elevated for longer or potentially tightening further. Kent's remarks come as the RBA considers its next move following the September rate increase, which was driven by persistent inflation, higher energy costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East, and ongoing capacity constraints in the economy. He noted that household demand is weakening, even as business credit growth remains robust, and that recent changes to housing-related taxes are helping to restrain activity in the property sector. On the labour market, Kent urged caution in interpreting volatile monthly data but acknowledged signs of easing conditions. Employment fell in September, and the unemployment rate rose to 4.7%, its highest level in five years. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: Heating Oil Falls on Prospects for More Russian Fuel

Trump framed the decision as a step to advance peace talks with Moscow, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration would review its economic consequences over the next 60 days. Still, supply risks remained elevated. Attacks on commercial vessels disrupted traffic through the Persian Gulf, and crude shipments fell to roughly 8.5 million barrels per day last week, down from more than 20 million barrels per day the week before, according to Kpler. Regional tensions intensified further after Egypt said it was prepared to back Saudi Arabia against Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement. At the same time, US fundamentals continued to signal tightness. EIA data showed that US distillate stocks declined by 2.5 million barrels in the week ending October 9, leaving inventories 12% below their five-year average and underscoring ongoing supply constraints. title: Euro Weakens as Violent Protests Hit Europe
body: The euro weakened as much as 0.5% to $1.118 on Monday before paring some of its losses, pressured by a wave of protests across France and other European countries that escalated into violent confrontations between police and demonstrators over the weekend. The unrest, which spread to major cities in Belgium, Italy, and Portugal, further undermined sentiment toward the single currency. At the same time, Moscow and Kyiv continued to strike energy infrastructure, with Ukrainian attacks setting ablaze an oil export terminal and a storage facility in St. Petersburg on Sunday, amplifying geopolitical uncertainty. Rising energy prices threatened to curb economic growth while keeping inflationary pressures elevated across Europe, leaving the euro exposed to additional downside if tensions deepen. The currency has been under sustained pressure since September amid mounting concerns over France's fiscal outlook and the European Central Bank's cautious approach to raising interest rates. title: Australian Shares Hover at Over 5-Week High as Week Opens
body: Australian equities advanced 33 points, or 0.4%, to 8,838 in early Monday trade, extending prior gains and reaching their highest level in more than five weeks. Risk sentiment improved on the back of a rebound in U.S. equity futures following last week's chip-sector selloff, as investors shifted their attention to the upcoming earnings season amid growing scrutiny of the AI sector. Domestically, softer-than-expected labour market data tempered expectations for an imminent rate hike by the Reserve Bank, lending additional support to the market. However, upside was capped by caution ahead of key data releases from major trading partner China later today, including September activity figures, home price data, and third-quarter GDP. Gains were led by the energy minerals and industrial services sectors, with notable advances from Nextdc Ltd. (up 3.6%), AGL Energy (up 1.7%), and Whitehaven Coal (up 1.2%). Challenger Ltd. jumped 14.5% after TAL Dai-ichi Life was reported to have made a non-binding takeover proposal at AUD 11.80 per share. The four major banks rose between 0.9% and 1.3%. title: US Futures Rise Ahead of Busy Earnings Week
body: US stock futures rose on Monday as investors geared up for a busy week of corporate earnings and reassessed the outlook for AI‑related investments. Nasdaq 100 futures advanced 0.7%, while S&P 500 and Dow futures each gained about 0.4%. Market participants are awaiting results from major companies including Tesla, Meta, Netflix, American Express, and GE Aerospace. The upbeat futures followed a difficult week for equities: the Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.48% and the S&P 500 fell 1.95% as technology shares came under pressure amid mounting concerns over AI financing. CoreWeave, a "neocloud" company that relies heavily on debt to fund data centers leased to technology firms, has become a key focus of these worries. Its shares tumbled 25% over the past week, while corporate bond investors have begun shunning its debt, driving the cost of its credit default swaps to distressed levels. title: New Zealand Private Sector Growth Hits 3-Month High
body: The BusinessNZ Performance of Composite Index rose to 53.4 in September 2026, up from a slightly revised 52.4 in August, marking a fourth consecutive month of expansion. This was the highest reading since June, reflecting faster growth in the manufacturing sector alongside continued expansion in services. Manufacturing activity strengthened despite headwinds from elevated fuel costs and uncertainty ahead of the general election. By contrast, services growth moderated slightly as the pace of new orders slowed. Among the sub-indices, stocks recorded faster expansion, while activity/sales returned to growth. In opposition to this, supplier deliveries and employment remained in contraction. The latest result underscores that cost-of-living pressures, fuel prices, interest rates, and election-related uncertainty continue to weigh heavily on sentiment.
